claim: Influenza A virus (IAV) infects 5–15% of the world's population every year.
source: Every year influenza A virus (IAV) infects 5–15% of the world's population (Goeijenbier et al., 2017; Stöhr, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Goeijenbier et al., 2017 and Stöhr, 2002

claim: Diabetes mellitus is a susceptibility factor for severe influenza virus infections.
source: Diabetes mellitus is a known susceptibility factor for severe influenza virus infections.
evidence: Stated in the abstract and supported by subsequent citations in the introduction

claim: Patients with diabetes have triple the risk of hospitalisation upon infection with influenza virus compared to individuals with no underlying illness.
source: Upon infection with influenza virus, patients with diabetes have triple the risk of hospitalisation, quadruple the risk of admission to the intensive care unit and double the risk of a fatal outcome compared to individuals with no underlying illness (Allard et al., 2010; Wilking et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allard et al., 2010 and Wilking et al., 2010

claim: Patients with diabetes have quadruple the risk of admission to the intensive care unit upon infection with influenza virus compared to individuals with no underlying illness.
source: Upon infection with influenza virus, patients with diabetes have triple the risk of hospitalisation, quadruple the risk of admission to the intensive care unit and double the risk of a fatal outcome compared to individuals with no underlying illness (Allard et al., 2010; Wilking et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allard et al., 2010 and Wilking et al., 2010

claim: Patients with diabetes have double the risk of a fatal outcome upon infection with influenza virus compared to individuals with no underlying illness.
source: Upon infection with influenza virus, patients with diabetes have triple the risk of hospitalisation, quadruple the risk of admission to the intensive care unit and double the risk of a fatal outcome compared to individuals with no underlying illness (Allard et al., 2010; Wilking et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allard et al., 2010 and Wilking et al., 2010

claim: Type I diabetes (T1D) accounts for approximately 10% of diabetes cases.
source: T1D accounts for ~10% of cases (Chatterjee et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Chatterjee et al., 2017

claim: Type I diabetes is generally regarded as an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells.
source: T1D accounts for ~10% of cases (Chatterjee et al., 2017) and is generally regarded as an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system attacks the insulin-producing pancreatic β-cells (Brody, 2012; Federation ID, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brody, 2012 and Federation ID, 2015

claim: Type II diabetes (T2D) accounts for approximately 90% of diabetes cases.
source: The remaining ~90% of cases belong to the T2D category which is characterised by relative insulin deficiency as a result of pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Defronzo, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2017 and Defronzo, 2009

claim: Type II diabetes is characterised by relative insulin deficiency as a result of pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance.
source: The remaining ~90% of cases belong to the T2D category which is characterised by relative insulin deficiency as a result of pancreatic β-cell dysfunction and insulin resistance (Chatterjee et al., 2017; Defronzo, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chatterjee et al., 2017 and Defronzo, 2009

claim: People with diabetes have a two- to fourfold increased risk of cardiovascular disease compared to healthy individuals.
source: Notably, when compared to healthy individuals, people with diabetes have a two- to fourfold increased risk of cardiovascular disease (Rao Kondapally Seshasai et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rao Kondapally Seshasai et al., 2011

claim: Elevated blood glucose levels in patients with diabetes are associated with kidney damage and the development of diabetic kidney disease.
source: Similarly, elevated blood glucose levels in patients with diabetes are associated with kidney damage and the development of diabetic kidney disease (Carpentier et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carpentier et al., 2018

claim: Hyperglycaemia is associated with increased susceptibility to infectious diseases.
source: In addition to being associated with the micro- and macrovascular complications of diabetes, hyperglycaemia is also associated with the increased susceptibility to infectious diseases (Critchley et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Critchley et al., 2018

claim: In a Danish population, each 1 mmol/L increase in plasma glucose level was associated with a 6% increased risk of hospitalisation for pneumonia.
source: For example, in a Danish population, each 1 mmol/L increase in plasma glucose level was associated with a 6% increased risk of hospitalisation for pneumonia (Benfield et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benfield et al., 2007

claim: Hyperglycaemia may increase IAV disease severity via immunosuppression.
source: In the specific case of IAV, hyperglycaemia may increase disease severity via either; immunosuppression (Reading et al., 1998), increased epithelial infection (Kohio and Adamson, 2013) and/or, altered activity of transporters responsible for keeping the lung free of oedematous fluid (Yamashita et al., 1992; Rivelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reading et al., 1998

claim: Hyperglycaemia may increase IAV disease severity via increased epithelial infection.
source: In the specific case of IAV, hyperglycaemia may increase disease severity via either; immunosuppression (Reading et al., 1998), increased epithelial infection (Kohio and Adamson, 2013) and/or, altered activity of transporters responsible for keeping the lung free of oedematous fluid (Yamashita et al., 1992; Rivelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohio and Adamson, 2013

claim: Hyperglycaemia may increase IAV disease severity via altered activity of transporters responsible for keeping the lung free of oedematous fluid.
source: In the specific case of IAV, hyperglycaemia may increase disease severity via either; immunosuppression (Reading et al., 1998), increased epithelial infection (Kohio and Adamson, 2013) and/or, altered activity of transporters responsible for keeping the lung free of oedematous fluid (Yamashita et al., 1992; Rivelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yamashita et al., 1992 and Rivelli et al., 2012

claim: Hyperglycaemia contributes to the elevated severity of enteric infections in patients with diabetes by increasing the permeability of the gut epithelium.
source: Thaiss and colleagues recently showed that hyperglycaemia contributes to the elevated severity of enteric infections in patients with diabetes by increasing the permeability of the gut epithelium (Thaiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thaiss et al., 2018

claim: GLUT2, a bidirectional glucose transporter, was identified as a key driver of dysfunction of the epithelial junctional complex.
source: Specifically, GLUT2, a bidirectional glucose transporter, was identified as a key driver of dysfunction of the epithelial junctional complex (Thaiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thaiss et al., 2018

claim: The epithelial junctional complex plays an important role in the lung by limiting the amount of fluid present in the alveolar airspace.
source: In addition to their role in the gut, the epithelial junctional complex plays an important role in the lung by limiting the amount of fluid present in the alveolar airspace.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about lung physiology

claim: The epithelial cell component of junctional proteins plays a more significant role than endothelial cells in keeping the lung free of fluid.
source: Junctional proteins are formed between both pulmonary epithelial cells and pulmonary endothelial cells, although the epithelial cell component plays a more significant role keeping the lung free of fluid (Short et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Short et al., 2014

claim: IAV can damage junctional proteins between adjacent human alveolar epithelial cells and therefore impair efficient gas-exchange.
source: We have previously demonstrated that IAV can damage junctional proteins between adjacent human alveolar epithelial cells and therefore impair efficient gas-exchange (Short et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Short et al., 2016

claim: High glucose co-cultures had a significantly greater decrease in TEER following IAV infection compared to low glucose co-cultures.
source: Strikingly, following IAV infection, high glucose co-cultures had a significantly greater decrease in TEER compared to low glucose co-cultures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Infected high glucose co-cultures had increased permeability to FITC-labeled dextran relative to infected low glucose co-cultures.
source: These data were consistent with the increased permeability to FITC-labeled dextran observed in infected high glucose co-cultures relative to infected low glucose co-cultures (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: No statistically significant difference in viral messenger RNA was observed between high and low glucose co-culture conditions.
source: However, no statistically significant difference in viral messenger RNA (mRNA) or infectious virus in supernatant was observed between the different glucose conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: No statistically significant difference in infectious virus in supernatant was observed between high and low glucose co-culture conditions.
source: However, no statistically significant difference in viral messenger RNA (mRNA) or infectious virus in supernatant was observed between the different glucose conditions (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells exposed to high glucose concentrations have an increased level of apoptosis compared to cells in lower glucose concentrations.
source: Human umbilical vein endothelial cells exposed to high glucose concentrations have an increased level of apoptosis compared to cells in lower glucose concentrations (Risso et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Risso et al., 2001

claim: No significant difference in LDH levels was observed in cells from high and low glucose co-cultures.
source: While LDH levels cannot definitively rule out a role of cell death, no significant difference was observed in cells from the high and low glucose co-cultures (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: A history of high glucose increases the IAV-induced damage to the epithelial-endothelial barrier in vitro in the absence of wide-spread cell death or increased viral replication.
source: Together, these data suggest that a history of high glucose increases the IAV-induced damage to the epithelial-endothelial barrier in vitro in the absence of wide-spread cell death or increased viral replication.
evidence: Inference drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1

claim: Endothelial cells provide a stabilising effect on the integrity of the epithelial barrier.
source: However, endothelial cells provided a stabilising effect on the integrity of the epithelial barrier (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with co-cultures having a significantly higher pre-infection TEER when compared to epithelial mono-cultures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Co-cultures have a significantly higher pre-infection TEER when compared to epithelial mono-cultures.
source: However, endothelial cells provided a stabilising effect on the integrity of the epithelial barrier (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), with co-cultures having a significantly higher pre-infection TEER when compared to epithelial mono-cultures.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Infected high glucose mono-cultures showed no statistically significant decrease in TEER overtime compared to infected low glucose mono-cultures.
source: Following IAV infection, infected high glucose mono-cultures showed no statistically significant decrease in TEER overtime compared to infected low glucose mono-cultures (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: No difference in epithelial permeability to FITC-labelled dextran was observed between high and low glucose mono-cultures.
source: Similarly, no difference in epithelial permeability to FITC-labelled dextran was observed (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Endothelial cells are the main drivers of barrier damage observed in the in vitro co-culture model under high glucose conditions.
source: Thus, given that high glucose IAV-induced barrier damage was not observed in the absence of endothelial cells, these data suggest that endothelial cells are the main drivers of barrier damage observed in this in vitro model.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparing co-culture and mono-culture experimental results

claim: Numerous differentially expressed genes were identified in endothelial cells derived from infected co-cultures relative to endothelial cells derived from uninfected co-cultures at 24 hr post-IAV infection.
source: At 24 hr post-IAV infection, numerous differentially expressed genes were identified in endothelial cells derived from infected co-cultures relative to endothelial cells derived from uninfected co-cultures (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Many genes were differentially expressed after infection under both low and high glucose conditions.
source: Many of these genes were differentially expressed after infection under both low and high glucose conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Certain pathways that were enriched in endothelial cells derived from infected, low glucose co-cultures were not enriched in endothelial cells derived from infected, high glucose co-cultures.
source: Strikingly, certain pathways that were enriched in endothelial cells derived from infected, low glucose co-cultures were not enriched in endothelial cells derived from infected, high glucose co-cultures (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: High glucose endothelial cells lacked a concomitant increase in regulatory pathways otherwise seen in low glucose endothelial cells.
source: Namely, while both low and high glucose endothelial cells expressed pathways associated with 'defence response to virus' and 'immune system processes', high glucose endothelial cells lacked a concomitant increase in regulatory pathways otherwise seen in low glucose endothelial cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by pathway analysis data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Endothelial cells derived from infected high glucose co-cultures may be in a more pro-inflammatory state than their counterparts in low glucose conditions.
source: These data suggest that endothelial cells derived from infected high glucose co-cultures may be in a more pro-inflammatory state than their counterparts in low glucose conditions.
evidence: Inference drawn from the pathway analysis data

claim: Endothelial cells from IAV-infected high glucose co-cultures expressed significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory chemokine CXCL8 compared to endothelial cells from IAV-infected low glucose co-cultures.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, endothelial cells from IAV-infected high glucose co-cultures expressed significantly higher levels of pro-inflammatory chemokine CXCL8 compared to endothelial cells from IAV-infected low glucose co-cultures (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3D

claim: An increase in IL-6 and IL-8 protein levels was observed in endothelial supernatant 24 hr post-infection in high glucose conditions.
source: Similarly, we observed an increase in IL-6 and IL-8 protein levels in endothelial supernatant 24 hr post-infection (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 3E

claim: The transfer of cell culture supernatant from high-glucose, infected co-cultures was sufficient to induce barrier damage in uninfected cells when compared to normal glucose conditions.
source: The transfer of the cell culture supernatant from high-glucose, infected co-cultures was sufficient to induce barrier damage in uninfected cells when compared to normal glucose conditions (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by supernatant transfer experiment data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The transfer of heat-treated supernatant from high glucose conditions did not damage the epithelial-endothelial barrier.
source: Consistent with a heat-labile soluble protein (such as a cytokine) driving the observed phenotype, the transfer of heat-treated supernatant from high glucose conditions did not damage the epithelial-endothelial barrier (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by heat-treated supernatant transfer experiment data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Infection using ultraviolet inactivated virus did not induce barrier damage, even under hyperglycaemic conditions.
source: Furthermore, infection using ultraviolet inactivated virus did not induce barrier damage, even under hyperglycaemic conditions, indicating that initially, active virus is required to induce a reduction in TEER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by UV-inactivated virus experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Active virus is required to induce a reduction in TEER.
source: Furthermore, infection using ultraviolet inactivated virus did not induce barrier damage, even under hyperglycaemic conditions, indicating that initially, active virus is required to induce a reduction in TEER (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inference drawn from UV-inactivated virus experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: vRNA and mRNA remains present up to 70°C.
source: These data suggest that the observed TEER decrease is not due to the presence of viral PAMPS/antigen in the media as it has been previously demonstrated that vRNA and mRNA remains present up to 70°C (Jonges et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jonges et al., 2010

claim: IL-1β is known to increase interstitial epithelial barrier permeability.
source: IL-1β is known to increase interstitial epithelial barrier permeability (Al-Sadi and Ma, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al-Sadi and Ma, 2007

claim: No difference in barrier integrity with and without Anakinra was observed.
source: No difference in barrier integrity with and without Anakinra was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that while the phenotype is likely due to a soluble factor, it is not IL-1 dependent.
evidence: Supported by Anakinra treatment experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The barrier damage phenotype is likely due to a soluble factor but is not IL-1 dependent.
source: No difference in barrier integrity with and without Anakinra was observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that while the phenotype is likely due to a soluble factor, it is not IL-1 dependent.
evidence: Inference drawn from Anakinra treatment experiment data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: A pro-inflammatory environment is known to facilitate the damage of the junctional complex between adjacent epithelial cells and increase barrier permeability.
source: A pro-inflammatory environment is known to facilitate the damage of the junctional complex between adjacent epithelial cells and increase barrier permeability (Short et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Short et al., 2014

claim: Hyperglycaemia can damage the integrity of junctional complex between epithelial cells in the gut.
source: Similarly, hyperglycaemia can damage the integrity of junctional complex between epithelial cells in the gut (Thaiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thaiss et al., 2018

claim: No difference in epithelial E-cadherin staining was observed between low and high glucose co-cultures.
source: No difference in epithelial E-cadherin staining was observed between low and high glucose co-cultures (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Infected high glucose co-cultures had significantly lower levels of Claudin-4 between adjacent epithelial cells compared to infected low glucose co-cultures.
source: However, infected high glucose co-cultures had significantly lower levels of Claudin-4 and JAM-1 between adjacent epithelial cells compared to infected low glucose co-cultures (Figure 4B & C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Infected high glucose co-cultures had significantly lower levels of JAM-1 between adjacent epithelial cells compared to infected low glucose co-cultures.
source: However, infected high glucose co-cultures had significantly lower levels of Claudin-4 and JAM-1 between adjacent epithelial cells compared to infected low glucose co-cultures (Figure 4B & C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Barrier damage occurred in both infected and bystander cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis that a soluble factor is driving the loss of barrier integrity, co-staining of Claudin-4 and the influenza A nucleoprotein demonstrate that barrier damage occurred in both infected and bystander cells (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by co-staining immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D

claim: There was no difference in junctional integrity of IAV-infected epithelial cells in low or high glucose mono-cultures.
source: In contrast to the co-cultures, there was no difference in junctional integrity of IAV-infected epithelial cells in low or high glucose mono-cultures (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5

claim: Under conditions of high glucose in vitro, active IAV triggers a pro-inflammatory response in endothelial cells which in turn damages the epithelial junctional complex.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that under conditions of high glucose in vitro, active IAV triggers a pro-inflammatory response in endothelial cells which in turn damages the epithelial junctional complex.
evidence: Inference drawn from the combined experimental data on endothelial inflammation and epithelial junctional damage

claim: Homozygote leprdb/db mice are obese and hyperglycaemic whilst their heterozygote (leprdb/+) counterparts are not.
source: To this end, we employed a well-established murine model of T2D where homozygote mice (leprdb/db) are obese and hyperglycaemic whilst their heterozygote (leprdb/+) counterparts are not (Kodama et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kodama et al., 1994

claim: Hyperglycaemia in leprdb/db mice was confirmed with a blood glucose test prior to infection.
source: Hyperglycaemia in leprdb/db mice was confirmed with a blood glucose test prior to infection (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by blood glucose measurement data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Weight-loss is not a clear marker for IAV disease severity of leptin receptor-deficient mice.
source: As demonstrated previously, weight-loss is not a clear marker for IAV disease severity of leptin receptor-deficient mice (Radigan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Radigan et al., 2014

claim: leprdb/db mice showed less weight loss than their leprdb/+ counterparts.
source: Consistent with these results, leprdb/db mice showed less weight loss than their leprdb/+ counterparts (data not shown).
evidence: Stated as observed data (though not shown)

claim: Pulse-oximetry is a non-invasive measure of lung injury.
source: It is well recognised that pulse-oximetry is a non-invasive measure of lung injury (Lax et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lax et al., 2014

claim: Blood oxygen saturation more accurately predicts disease severity than systemic weight loss in the case of murine influenza studies.
source: It is well recognised that pulse-oximetry is a non-invasive measure of lung injury (Lax et al., 2014) that more accurately predicts disease severity than systemic weight loss in the case of murine influenza studies (Verhoeven et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Verhoeven et al., 2009

claim: IAV-infected leprdb/db mice had significantly lower blood oxygen saturation at three days post-infection compared to leprdb/+ mice.
source: IAV-infected leprdb/db mice had significantly lower blood oxygen saturation at three days post-infection compared to leprdb/+ mice (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by pulse oximetry data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Lower blood oxygen saturation in IAV-infected leprdb/db mice was not associated with an increase in infectious virus present.
source: Consistent with our in vitro data this was not associated with an increase in infectious virus present (Figure 6C)
evidence: Supported by viral titration data shown in Figure 6C

claim: There was a difference in viral messenger RNA (mRNA) between the homozygote and heterozygote mice.
source: Consistent with our in vitro data this was not associated with an increase in infectious virus present (Figure 6C); however, there was difference in viral messenger RNA (mRNA) between the homozygote and heterozygote mice (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Infected hyperglycaemic leprdb/db mice had a significant reduction in JAM-1 levels between adjacent pulmonary epithelial cells compared to normoglycaemic leprdb/+ mice.
source: Strikingly, and also consistent with our in vitro data, infected hyperglycaemic leprdb/db mice had a significant reduction in both JAM-1 and Claudin-4 levels between adjacent pulmonary epithelial cells compared to normoglycaemic leprdb/+ mice (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E and 6G

claim: Infected hyperglycaemic leprdb/db mice had a significant reduction in Claudin-4 levels between adjacent pulmonary epithelial cells compared to normoglycaemic leprdb/+ mice.
source: Strikingly, and also consistent with our in vitro data, infected hyperglycaemic leprdb/db mice had a significant reduction in both JAM-1 and Claudin-4 levels between adjacent pulmonary epithelial cells compared to normoglycaemic leprdb/+ mice (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F and 6G

claim: IAV-infected leprdb/db mice had higher levels of pulmonary pro-inflammatory cytokines than infected leprdb/+ mice.
source: Consistent with our in vitro findings, IAV-infected leprdb/db mice had higher levels of pulmonary pro-inflammatory cytokines than infected leprdb/+ mice, although this often just fell short of statistical significance (e.g. IP-10, p=0.06).
evidence: Supported by cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 6H

claim: Loss of intact tight junctions in the context of IAV and hyperglycaemia is associated with a pro-inflammatory response.
source: Whilst we cannot offer definitive evidence that these cytokines were endothelial cell derived (as was the case with the in vitro data), these data are consistent with our in vitro data that loss of intact tight junctions in the context of IAV and hyperglycaemia is associated with a pro-inflammatory response.
evidence: Inference drawn from the in vivo cytokine and tight junction data

claim: Diabetes increases the risk of developing severe influenza.
source: It is well established that diabetes increases the risk of developing severe influenza (Hulme et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hulme et al., 2017

claim: Elevated glucose levels are associated with endothelial cell inflammation, destruction of the epithelial junctional complex and increased IAV severity.
source: Here, we show that elevated glucose levels are associated with endothelial cell inflammation, destruction of the epithelial junctional complex and increased IAV severity.
evidence: Summary of the experimental findings from the study

claim: In patients with hyperglycaemia, IAV triggers a pronounced inflammatory response in pulmonary endothelial cells.
source: We therefore propose that in patients with hyperglycaemia, IAV triggers a pronounced inflammatory response in pulmonary endothelial cells.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the study's findings

claim: Secreted protein components of the inflammatory response (most likely cytokines) damage the epithelial junctional complex and worsen IAV-induced barrier damage.
source: Secreted protein components of this inflammatory response (most likely cytokines) then damage the epithelial junctional complex and worsen IAV-induced barrier damage.
evidence: Proposed mechanism based on the study's findings

claim: Elevated blood glucose levels can directly increase glucose concentrations in airway secretions.
source: Elevated blood glucose levels can directly increase glucose concentrations in airway secretions (Philips et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Philips et al., 2003

claim: Exposure of epithelial cells to elevated glucose concentrations facilitates increased IAV replication by augmenting the assembly and activity of the cellular vacuolar-type H+ ATPase (V-ATPase).
source: Exposure of epithelial cells to elevated glucose concentrations then facilitates increased IAV replication by augmenting the assembly and activity of the cellular vacuolar-type H+ ATPase (V-ATPase) (Kohio and Adamson, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kohio and Adamson, 2013

claim: Hyperglycaemia increased IAV-induced barrier damage in vitro and increased influenza severity in vivo in the absence of increased viral replication.
source: Interestingly, in the present study, we observed that hyperglycaemia increased IAV-induced barrier damage in vitro and increased influenza severity in vivo in the absence of increased viral replication (although initial viral replication was required to trigger epithelial barrier damage).
evidence: Summary of the study's findings

claim: Initial viral replication was required to trigger epithelial barrier damage.
source: Interestingly, in the present study, we observed that hyperglycaemia increased IAV-induced barrier damage in vitro and increased influenza severity in vivo in the absence of increased viral replication (although initial viral replication was required to trigger epithelial barrier damage).
evidence: Inference from the UV-inactivated virus experiment

claim: Elevated glucose levels can directly affect the activity of ATPases in epithelial cells.
source: Interestingly, previous studies have described elevated glucose levels can directly affect the activity of ATPases in epithelial cells (Kohio and Adamson, 2013; Yamashita et al., 1992; Rivelli et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kohio and Adamson, 2013; Yamashita et al., 1992; Rivelli et al., 2012

claim: The Na,K-ATPase (located on the basolateral side of pulmonary epithelial cells) has been implicated in the pathogenesis of influenza virus.
source: This is of interest given that the Na,K-ATPase (located on the basolateral side of pulmonary epithelial cells) has been implicated in the pathogenesis of influenza virus (Peteranderl et al., 2016; van de Sandt et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peteranderl et al., 2016 and van de Sandt et al., 2017

claim: Altering the activity of the Na,K-ATPase pump can facilitate pulmonary oedema.
source: Altering the activity of this pump can not only facilitate pulmonary oedema, but it can also affect the formation of the junctional complex between adjacent epithelial cells (Rajasekaran and Rajasekaran, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rajasekaran and Rajasekaran, 2003

claim: Altering the activity of the Na,K-ATPase pump can affect the formation of the junctional complex between adjacent epithelial cells.
source: Altering the activity of this pump can not only facilitate pulmonary oedema, but it can also affect the formation of the junctional complex between adjacent epithelial cells (Rajasekaran and Rajasekaran, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rajasekaran and Rajasekaran, 2003

claim: Numerous different cytokines, including TNF-α, CXCL8, TNF-β, IFN-γ and IL-6, have been reported to damage the tight junctions of epithelial cells.
source: Numerous different cytokines, including TNF-α, CXCL8, TNF-β, IFN-γ and IL-6, have been reported to damage the tight junctions of epithelial cells (van de Sandt et al., 2017; Ohkuni et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to van de Sandt et al., 2017; Ohkuni et al., 2011; Shen et al., 2017

claim: A combination of TNF-α and IFN-γ can reduce the integrity of the epithelial barrier via inhibition of the Na,K-ATPase.
source: Indeed, we have previously demonstrated that a combination TNF-α and IFN-γ can reduce the integrity of the epithelial barrier via inhibition of the Na,K-ATPase (van de Sandt et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to van de Sandt et al., 2017

claim: Hyperglycaemia, through GLUT2-dependent transcriptional reprogramming of epithelial cells, facilitated intestinal tight junction dysfunction.
source: Thaiss and colleagues recently showed that hyperglycaemia, through GLUT2-dependent transcriptional reprogramming of epithelial cells, facilitated intestinal tight junction dysfunction (Thaiss et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thaiss et al., 2018

claim: The epithelial cells in the present study were only indirectly exposed to differential glucose levels.
source: However, it is important to recognise that in contrast to the work of Thaiss and colleagues, the epithelial cells in the present study were only indirectly exposed to differential glucose levels (i.e. differing glucose concentrations were restricted to the lower chamber of the co-culture).
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: The endothelial cells in the present study only differed in their history of glucose exposure, and all in vitro groups were exposed to the same glucose concentration at the time of IAV infection.
source: Moreover, unlike the study of Thaiss et al., 2018 the endothelial cells in the present study only differed in their history of glucose exposure, and all in vitro groups were exposed to the same glucose concentration at the time of IAV infection.
evidence: Description of the experimental design

claim: The data presented are congruent with the so-called 'legacy effect' described in patients with diabetes.
source: Therefore, the data presented here are more congruent with the so-called 'legacy effect' described in patients with diabetes.
evidence: Inference connecting the study findings to the legacy effect concept

claim: The legacy effect has been used to explain the observation that the detrimental effects of elevated glucose levels in patients persist beyond the period of hyperglycaemia.
source: The legacy effect has been used to explain the observation that the detrimental effects of elevated glucose levels in patients persist beyond the period of hyperglycaemia (Chen et al., 2016; El-Osta et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; El-Osta et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2014

claim: Epigenetic changes (which persist even after transient hyperglycaemia) influence the regulation of NF-κB.
source: Why the legacy effect occurs is unclear but it has been proposed that epigenetic changes (which persist even after transient hyperglycaemia) influence the regulation of NF-κB (Chen et al., 2016; El-Osta et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016; El-Osta et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2014

claim: The physiological effects of changes in blood glucose levels can persist for up to 10 years.
source: Of particular concern are observations that the physiological effects of changes in blood glucose levels can persist for up to 10 years (Holman et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holman et al., 2008

claim: 1 in 11 adults are living with diabetes at present.
source: At present, 1 in 11 adults are living with diabetes.
evidence: Based on established epidemiological knowledge

claim: Within the next 20 years, the incidence of diabetes is expected to increase to 1 in 10 adults.
source: Within the next 20 years, this incidence is expected to increase to 1 in 10 adults (Sainsbury et al., 2018).
